summary: Moses assembles Israel, restates the Sabbath command, and calls for willing gifts and skilled work for the sanctuary. Men and women bring materials, women spin the fabrics, rulers supply stones and spices, and Moses identifies Bezalel and Oholiab as divinely equipped makers and teachers.
whyItMatters: After covenant renewal the people respond through shared giving and practical work. The chapter makes the contribution of women and the transmission of craft skills visible while placing the entire undertaking after the command to rest.

context.author: Exodus does not name its final author. It records Moses writing particular covenant material; traditional Mosaic attribution and modern accounts of composition are distinguished in the book briefing.
context.audience: Israel remembering its rescue from Egypt and its obligations as a covenant community. The chapter does not identify an individual dedicatee.
context.date: The narrative places these events at Sinai after the departure from Egypt. The date of the events and the history of the book’s composition are separate, debated questions.
context.setting: Israel's assembled camp after Moses returns from Sinai with renewed covenant instructions.
context.literaryForm: Assembly speech, an itemized call for materials and work, a report of communal response, and the makers' public commissioning.

before.text: Moses has returned with the renewed tablets, conveyed the commands, and established a pattern of speaking with God and the people. The community is now called together to undertake the sanctuary work.

here.text: The inventory of needed work becomes a report of actual gifts and skilled participation, with repeated emphasis on willing hearts.

after.text: The makers begin, the gifts exceed what is needed, and Moses stops the collection before the construction report describes the tent itself.

outline.heading: Sabbath before the work
outline.note: The assembly hears the rest command, its death sanction, and the prohibition on kindling fire.

outline.heading: Materials and tasks requested
outline.note: Willing gifts and skilled makers are called for every part of sanctuary service.

outline.heading: The community’s response
outline.note: Men, women, spinners, and rulers contribute materials and labor.

outline.heading: Bezalel and Oholiab as makers and teachers
outline.note: God-given skill includes both performing the work and teaching it.

keyVerses.text: They came, everyone whose heart stirred him up, and everyone whom his spirit made willing, and brought Yahweh’s offering for the work of the Tent of Meeting, and for all of its service, and for the holy garments.
keyVerses.why: The contribution report emphasizes people moved to give for the actual work of the sanctuary.

keyVerses.text: All the women who were wise-hearted spun with their hands, and brought that which they had spun: the blue, the purple, the scarlet, and the fine linen.
keyVerses.why: Women are explicitly identified as skilled producers of the spun material.

keyVerses.text: He has put in his heart that he may teach, both he and Oholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan.
keyVerses.why: The makers’ ability to teach makes the work more than the achievement of isolated craftsmen.

questions.question: Why does the construction call begin with Sabbath?
questions.answer: Before asking for gifts or labor, Moses reiterates the six-day work rhythm and seventh-day rest. Even this sacred project is introduced within the community's obligation to cease work.

questions.question: How severe is the opening Sabbath rule?
questions.answer: It states that working on the day carries death and adds a prohibition on kindling fire throughout the dwellings. Those sanctions and restrictions accompany the rest command as part of this ancient covenant setting.

questions.question: What does “willing heart” mean in the offering appeal?
questions.answer: It describes the people who choose to bring materials, and the report repeats that their hearts or spirits move them. The chapter does not assign one identical material contribution to every household.

questions.question: Do contributions consist only of precious metals?
questions.answer: They also include colored materials, linen, goats' hair, skins, wood, oil, spices, and stones. The list reflects the different needs of the structure, furnishings, clothing, light, and ritual mixtures.

questions.question: What work does the chapter specifically attribute to women?
questions.answer: Women bring gifts alongside men, and skilled women spin the colored material, linen, and goats' hair. The text explicitly recognizes both their donations and their labor in producing what the sanctuary requires.

questions.question: Why list so many objects before reporting the gifts?
questions.answer: The inventory identifies the scope of the task, from the tent and ark to court pins and priestly clothing. It allows the reader to connect apparently varied donations with a planned set of objects and services.

questions.question: How do Bezalel and Oholiab contribute beyond making objects?
questions.answer: Moses credits them with wisdom in many crafts and specifically with the ability to teach. Their commission therefore includes enabling others to participate in skilled work, alongside the work they personally perform.

glossary.def: The willingly brought contribution of materials for the sanctuary work.
Endowed with practical wisdom or skill, used here for makers and women who spin.
A skilled worker who cuts or marks designs in the materials used for the sanctuary.
